evals.prompt: We're a small team at Reticule shipping a hosted geocoding API - you POST an address and get back coordinates plus a confidence score. Public launch is in about five weeks and I need the getting-started page written. I want it to have an embedded StackBlitz sandbox, because a competitor's sandbox is literally why I tried them. Success for us = the developer has made their first API call and understands how our auth model and rate-limit tiers work. Right now getting a key means emailing our sales inbox and someone provisions a sandbox tenant for you, usually next business day. Docs infra isn't anyone's job here - we're four backend engineers and a founder who writes the blog.
evals.expected_output: An interview-grounded quickstart plan: a restated observable success moment, a 5-minute budget, a plain-page container with the sandbox struck from the shortlist, an escalation of the access mechanism above the sales-gated tenant, the four-part step shape, and a cold-run verification plan.
expectations: Rejects 'the developer has made their first API call' as the success moment because it names a step the reader performs rather than something the product visibly does.
Replaces it with an observable result, such as the response carrying coordinates for the address the reader just submitted.
Commits to a time budget of 5 minutes for this hosted-API quickstart.
Recommends a plain documentation page as the container instead of the embedded sandbox.
Identifies the embedded sandbox as the lowest-efficiency container: the most friction removed, but the highest build-and-upkeep effort.
Deletes the embedded sandbox from the shortlist entirely rather than ranking it last, because the team named no owner to keep it working.

Names the sales-inbox key provisioning as the dominant friction and asks for a higher access rung - no account at all, a temporary development key, or an instant self-serve key - before any signup step is written.
Presents the access mechanisms as a ranked ladder in which the sales-gated sandbox ranks last.
Keeps the auth-model and rate-limit-tier explanation out of the quickstart, routing it to explanation or reference documentation.
Specifies each step as a verb-led heading naming the whole outcome, exactly one copy-pasteable block, the expected output, and a one-line fail branch.
Delivers a cold-run verification plan naming the environment and who executes it, rather than a page with no verification attached.

evals.prompt: Our getting-started page for Halyard (a managed Postgres branching service) has been up for a year. Analytics say 62% of the people who load it never reach the 'create branch' call at the end. The page honestly looks fine to me and to the two engineers who wrote it - all three of us run through it without any trouble. Can you rewrite it so people actually finish? I'll paste the current page content if you need it but you can probably tell what's wrong from the structure: intro paragraph about branching, install CLI, auth, create project, create branch, next steps.
evals.expected_output: A cold-run-first audit: a defect table ordered by minutes lost with the rewritten page after it, plus the clean-environment protocol, a two-profile run, a friction log, and a 10-minute budget.
expectations: Cold-runs the existing page before rewriting anything, and states that rewriting from reading alone is not acceptable.
Returns a defect table whose rows carry the step number, what the page says, what actually happened, and the elapsed time at that point.
Orders the defect table by minutes lost.
Leads with the defects and places the rewritten page after them, presenting the rewrite as the fix rather than the finding.
Requires the cold run to happen on a clean environment with a fresh account, no cached credentials and no pre-installed dependencies.
Starts the timer at page load, not at the first command.
Treats any command the runner had to adjust to make work as a defect, rather than silently fixing it.
Treats an output that differs from the documented output as a defect even when the command still succeeded.
Requires a second run by a reader profile new to the ecosystem, distinct from one fluent in it, because the authors' own runs under-catch assumed knowledge.
Keeps a friction log beside the defect table, tagging each entry green for delight, yellow for friction, red for blocking.
Commits to a 10-minute budget for this database/data-platform product class.

evals.prompt: Quick question. Tessera is our CLI that compiles design tokens into platform-specific files. Our getting-started page runs to 14 numbered steps: install Homebrew, install the CLI, create an account, verify your email, run `tessera login`, create a workspace, invite a teammate, install the VS Code extension, create a tokens file, configure a build target, run the build, inspect the output, set up the CI action, and read the theming overview. Is that too long? I don't have a week to spend on this.
evals.expected_output: An audit only: per-step time attribution, a cut list ranked by minutes saved, the CLI budget and step-count rule, the artefact-on-disk success moment, and a scope cut rather than a longer budget.
expectations: Returns an audit only and does not emit a rewritten quickstart page.
Returns a step-by-step time attribution across the 14 listed steps.
Returns a cut list ranked by minutes saved.
Names 5 minutes as the baseline budget for a CLI quickstart.
States that a quickstart carries roughly three to six steps, and that 14 means the success moment is too large.
Defines the success moment as the compiled artefact on disk and requires the page to show its contents, for example an `ls` or `cat` of the generated file, not merely the build command's exit.
Cuts 'invite a teammate', 'install the VS Code extension', 'set up the CI action' and 'read the theming overview' as work the success moment does not need, naming where each one belongs instead.
Resolves the overrun by shrinking the success moment rather than raising the time budget.
Moves the surviving requirements (Homebrew, account, login) into a before-you-start block, each with a one-line check command, rather than leaving them as numbered steps.

evals.prompt: Grindstone is our hosted feature-flag API. The getting-started page is genuinely clean - we cold-ran it on a fresh laptop last month, it takes 6 minutes end to end, every command works, output matches. 71% of readers who start it reach the final step. But 30-day activation from docs signups has been flat at 3% for a year. Marketing wants to rewrite the page with a stronger hero section and an embedded video. What would you do?
evals.expected_output: A measurement deliverable, not an authoring one: success event and funnel definition, the drop-off questions to answer first, the KPI instrumentation order with day-7 return promoted, and a baseline-derived target.
expectations: Treats this as a measurement and instrumentation problem rather than an authoring one, and does not produce a rewritten page.
Defines the success event and the funnel steps to instrument.
Lists the drop-off questions the data must answer before any rewrite is commissioned.
Instruments step-level drop-off first, because every other page metric falls out of the same events.
Ranks support tickets or issues quoting a specific quickstart step above median time-to-success and completion rate.
Notes that median page-load-to-success time and completion rate tie, because both read the same start-and-success event pair and neither localises a defect.
Promotes day-7 return of completers above the cheaper metrics, specifically because completion is healthy while activation is flat.
States that day-7 return requires docs and product to share an identity, decided before publishing.
Raises the possibility that the chosen success moment itself is the wrong one, since no cheaper metric can establish that.
Sets any KPI target from the page's own baseline measured over roughly four weeks, as a relative improvement, and refuses to import a benchmark number from an outside vendor's blog.

evals.prompt:
Can you tidy up these two steps of our quickstart? Product is Quillpost, a transactional email API.

## Installing the client

Run `$ npm install` to pull in the client library.

## Configuring your credentials

Create a client with your key:

```
1  const qp = new Quillpost("qp_live_9fT2xA");
2  // your key is in Settings > API
```

## Sending your first email

```
await qp.send({ to: "dev@example.com", subject: "Hi", body: "Test" });
```

That's it! Now check out templates, webhooks, scheduling, batch sends, our Terraform provider, and the analytics dashboard.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten block set fixing every copy-paste defect: prompt and line numbers stripped, package named and pinned, an unmistakable test-scoped placeholder, full runnable file with imports, verb-led outcome headings, separate expected-output blocks, fail branches, and three next steps.
expectations: Removes the `$` shell prompt from the install command.
Names the package explicitly instead of a bare `npm install`, and pins a version.
Removes the line numbers from the code block.
Replaces `qp_live_9fT2xA` with an unmistakable placeholder such as `<YOUR_API_KEY>`, and states that a plausible-looking fake value gets pasted verbatim.
Flags the `live` scope of the key specifically and recommends a test-scoped key, so a copy-paste mistake cannot send real email or cost money.
Moves the `// your key is in Settings > API` commentary out of the copy-pasteable block, placing it immediately before or after.
Replaces the 'Settings > API' wording with a direct one-click link to the credential page.
Gives the complete runnable file including its `import` statement, rather than the fragment shown.
Rewrites each heading as a verb-led statement of the whole outcome and removes the `-ing` form.
Adds an expected-output block to each step, in a separate block from the command so the output cannot be copied along with it.
Adds a one-line fail branch to each step, tied to its most likely error.
Cuts the closing list to at most three next steps.

evals.prompt: Northgate is our observability SDK. We officially support TypeScript, Python, Go, Java, Ruby and Rust. Product wants all six as tabs on the getting-started page in time for our user conference in nine weeks. The docs site runs on Docusaurus. Realistically we'll only run the TypeScript path ourselves - the other five we'll generate from the TypeScript version and have each SDK owner eyeball them before we ship. Can you set that up?
evals.expected_output: A refusal of eyeball-only verification, a reduction from six tabs toward two or three or separate pages, synchronized tab groups, the per-release cold-run cost, the branching-is-not-a-tab rule, and a 10-minute SDK budget.
expectations: Refuses the eyeball-only verification and requires every tab to be cold-run independently.
States that each tab is its own quickstart sharing a layout, and that an unverified tab is worse than a missing one because the reader trusts it identically.
Flags six tabs as too many, naming two or three genuine first-class languages as the practical limit.
Reads the demand for six tabs as a signal the page is serving audiences that want different success moments, and offers separate per-language pages as the alternative.
Requires the tab groups on the page to be synchronized through a shared group identifier, so choosing a language once switches every remaining block and persists across visits.
Names the recurring cost of tabs as re-running every tab each release, not the one-time wiring.
Distinguishes parallel language variants from real conditional branching such as a proxy or firewall path, and routes real branching to a how-to guide rather than a tab.
Places language tabs in the middle of the container ranking and confirms the plain page remains the default.
Asks whether the page is a one-off launch asset or a compounding one, and ties the synchronized switcher and CI-run commands to the compounding answer.
Commits to a 10-minute baseline budget for this SDK/library quickstart.
Keeps the same success moment, step shape and verification across every language variant.

evals.prompt: Ferrous is our on-prem data-masking engine. Banks and insurers buy it. On my laptop the quickstart takes about 4 minutes: pull the image, run it, curl the health endpoint, mask a sample record. But our field engineers say new customers take two to four weeks to get through that same page, and the single most common support ticket is literally 'stuck at step 1'. Make the page faster.
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that access, not code, is the bottleneck: an upfront provisioning block with named owners, air-gapped command variants, pinned image tags, resource prerequisites, the self-hosted budget, and an identical success moment.
expectations: Identifies access provisioning rather than the code path as the bottleneck, stating that a 4-minute code path is wrapped in a multi-week access path the page never mentions.
Adds an upfront block naming exactly what must exist before step 1, such as tenant or licence, sandbox environment, role or permission, and allow-listed network or registry egress.
Names who inside the customer's own organisation provisions each of those items.
Rejects any 'contact your administrator' instruction that does not state exactly what to ask for.
Supplies an offline or air-gapped variant of every command that assumes internet access, including the image pull.
Keeps the success moment, step shape and verification identical to the self-serve version, changing only the access path.
Pins the container image tag rather than using a floating tag.
States resource requirements such as CPU, memory and disk as prerequisites, instead of letting the reader discover them mid-run.
Uses 30 to 60 minutes as the baseline budget for this self-hosted infrastructure quickstart, rather than carrying over the author's 4-minute laptop figure.
Treats the 'stuck at step 1' tickets as a signal localising an ambiguous instruction to a specific sentence, and uses them as an input to the fix.
Requires the cold run on a clean machine with a freshly provisioned tenant and no cached credentials, not the author's laptop.

evals.prompt: Cobalt is our columnar analytics database. The getting-started page runs about 2,600 words and roughly 70% of it is environment setup: pinning a Python version, installing a JDBC driver, getting a compatible Arrow build, installing our CLI. Then three steps to query a public taxi-trip dataset we host, and the payoff is a bar chart of trips per hour. Our data-eng team wants to move the whole page into a hosted notebook instead. Nobody has volunteered to maintain notebook infrastructure, though our platform team already runs a JupyterHub for internal analysts.
evals.expected_output: Setup split onto its own page linked from step 1, prerequisites with check commands, the notebook promoted on the strength of the existing JupyterHub, the demo dataset replaced by reader-inserted rows, and a 10-minute budget.
expectations: Splits the environment setup onto its own page linked from step 1, rather than trimming it down inside the quickstart.
Justifies the split by noting readers need setup documentation long after they stop needing the quickstart.
Places every remaining prerequisite before step 1, each with a one-line check command and an install pointer.
States that any prerequisite discovered after step 1 during a cold run counts as a defect.
Recognises a chart, table or query result as the success moment that makes a notebook the fitting container.
Promotes the notebook above its default ranking specifically because the platform team already runs hosted notebook infrastructure, turning a standing job into near-free.
States that a notebook with no named owner would be deleted from the shortlist rather than ranked last.
Replaces the hosted public taxi dataset with rows the reader inserts during the quickstart and then queries, because a dataset the reader did not create weakens the proof.
Commits to a 10-minute baseline budget for this database/data-platform quickstart.

evals.prompt: Palisade is our API gateway SDK. The quickstart has broken silently twice this year - once when we renamed a config key in a minor release, once when an upstream dependency changed a default - and both times a customer found it before we did. I want this checked automatically. Separately: who should actually own writing these pages? Right now our one staff technical writer drafts all of them and she's about three weeks behind.
evals.expected_output: A CI regression job running the page's own blocks against the published artefact with throwaway tenants, scheduled runs and a release-blocking failure, plus a docs-as-code ownership model with the shipping engineer drafting.
expectations: Runs the quickstart's own command blocks verbatim in CI, rather than a hand-maintained parallel script.
Runs them against the published artefact - the released package and the public endpoint - not the repository working copy, because readers never have the working copy.
Requires executable blocks to be annotated in the page source so an extractor knows which blocks to run.
Asserts the documented outputs, normalising volatile fragments such as ids, timestamps and durations with patterns rather than deleting the assertion.
Provisions a throwaway account or tenant per run so credential state never leaks between runs.
Runs on a schedule as well as on release, because upstream dependency and hosted-API changes break the page with no commit in the repository.
Fails the release on a failing run rather than filing a ticket.
Justifies the hard failure by stating that an outdated quickstart is worse than a missing one, because it spends the reader's trust before it spends their time.
Makes the shipping engineer the first-draft author for a quickstart tied to one SDK or feature, since at merge time they alone know the exact commands and output.
Keeps the writer in a review role and proposes a merge gate blocking pull requests without docs, so features get documented while fresh.
Asks the team to agree a review cadence and a final-authority rule, rather than asserting a standard one already exists.

evals.prompt: Write the quickstart for Vellum, our managed vector store. Our target users are data analysts at mid-size insurers - most of them have never worked with embeddings or chunking before, so the page needs to teach those concepts first. While you're in there, our repo README is a mess too, and the docs site nav has grown to about 40 items with no obvious order. Budget is one afternoon.
evals.expected_output: A scope check splitting the three requests: the concept-teaching audience routed to a getting-started guide or tutorial, the README and navigation routed to their own named skills, and the quickstart kept to one contrived happy path.
expectations: Declines to cover all three requests in a single page and separates them into distinct pieces of work.
States that a quickstart's reader is a domain expert who knows the problem space and is new only to this product.
Routes the audience that must first learn embeddings and chunking to a getting-started guide or a teaching tutorial, instead of inlining the concepts.
Refuses to open the quickstart with concept or architecture prose, naming background before the first action as a defect.
Routes the README rewrite to the repository-landing-page skill rather than handling it inside the quickstart.
Routes the 40-item navigation problem to the documentation structure/information-architecture skill.
Names the specific sibling skills for those hand-offs rather than describing them vaguely.
Confirms that a quickstart deliberately teaches nothing general: one contrived happy path, no branching.
States that a quickstart drops detailed concept descriptions, walkthroughs of complex use cases, and explanations of why each step is performed.
Still puts prerequisites, versions and credential paths upfront, because 'domain expert' does not mean 'already set up'.
